opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find most interesting is that recurrence in depth separates how much a model knows from how much it computes. In a standard transformer, the number of layers is fixed, so every token gets the same amount of computation. It doesn't matter whether you're completing a trivial phrase or working through a hard reasoning problem. If you instead take a block of layers and apply it repeatedly, iterating in a latent space, you can scale the compute at test time without adding any parameters. You simply run the loop longer when the problem is harder.

Algorithmically, that changes what the model is learning. It's no longer just learning a function. It's closer to learning an iterative procedure, an update rule that refines its internal state step by step. That connects to a lot of classical ideas. You can think of it like fixed-point iteration, or an optimization algorithm unrolled in the forward pass. One of the hopes is that this kind of structure generalizes better. In some of our earlier work on things like mazes and prefix sums, we saw that a model trained with a small number of iterations on easy problems could solve much harder problems at test time just by thinking longer. That kind of extrapolation is really hard to get from a fixed-depth network.

Language models also do a version of this with chain-of-thought, but there all the intermediate reasoning has to be squeezed through discrete tokens. Recurrence lets the model reason in a continuous, high-dimensional latent space. It doesn't have to verbalize every step, it doesn't need specialized training data with reasoning traces, and it can potentially represent things that are awkward to put into words.

Then there are some nice emergent behaviors you get almost for free. Different tokens naturally converge at different speeds, so you get adaptive compute per token. You can exit early when the state stops changing. You can share or reuse caches across iterations. And when you look at the latent trajectories, you sometimes see really structured dynamics, like orbits or particular patterns when the model is doing something like arithmetic. That suggests the model is actually using the recurrence to compute, not just repeating the same thing. So for me it's a really rich space, both as an engineering lever for test-time scaling and as a window into what kinds of algorithms these networks can learn.

r001.rationale: It says to take a block of layers and apply it repeatedly, running the loop longer when needed.

r002.rationale: It explains that the model can run more recurrent computation in latent space without verbalizing each step, separating extra computation from output generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that I find really interesting is that if you look at a standard transformer, the amount of compute you spend on every token is fixed. Every token gets exactly the same number of layers, the same number of operations, whether it's a trivial token, like a comma, or whether it's the token where the model actually has to decide what the answer to a math problem is. And that's kind of a strange design choice if you think about it, right? It's just an artifact of how we build these things, not something that falls out of any principle about what reasoning should look like.

And so recurrence in depth is this very simple idea: instead of stacking more and more distinct layers, you take a block of layers and you just run it again. You iterate it. And the reason I find that algorithmically interesting is that now the depth of the model becomes a variable rather than a constant. You can train the model to run, say, a random number of iterations, and then at test time you can decide, okay, I'm going to run this for four iterations, or sixteen, or sixty-four, and ideally the model gets better as you give it more compute. So the model is learning something closer to an algorithm, something you can unroll for longer, rather than a fixed-size function.

There's a nice connection to classical ideas too. If you think about iterative solvers, gradient descent, fixed-point iteration, all of these are recurrent computations where you apply the same update over and over until you converge. And there's a line of work, including some I've been involved with, showing that recurrent networks trained on things like mazes or prefix sums can actually extrapolate, you can train on small problems and then run more iterations and solve bigger problems. That's the behavior you'd want from a system that's actually learned the algorithm and not just memorized the training distribution.

The other piece that I think is underappreciated is that this gives you a way to scale test-time compute that doesn't go through tokens. Right now the dominant way to make a model think harder is chain of thought: you make it produce more text. But that forces the model to verbalize everything, and it's bounded by what can be expressed in the vocabulary. With latent recurrence, the model can iterate in its hidden state, in a continuous space, and refine a representation without ever having to write it down. Whether that ultimately captures different kinds of reasoning than chain of thought does, I think that's a genuinely open and exciting question, and it's part of why I've been spending so much time on it.

r001.rationale: The response describes taking a block of layers and running it again repeatedly.

r002.rationale: It says the model can iterate in its hidden state and refine a representation without writing it down, explaining how added computation can happen without generating more output.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that recurrence lets you separate the amount of computation from the number of parameters. In a standard transformer, you have a fixed stack of layers, and each layer has its own weights. With recurrence in depth, you repeatedly apply the same block to a hidden state. So you can spend more computation on a problem without having to make the model larger.

That gives you a useful inductive bias for learning algorithms. If you think about an iterative algorithm, you usually have an update rule that you apply repeatedly. You don’t have a completely different rule for step seven and step eight. A recurrent model has that same structure: it can learn an operation that refines its internal representation over several steps.

The exciting question is whether it learns something that continues to be useful when you run it for more steps than it saw during training. That’s not automatic—repeating a block could just converge to something unhelpful. But if it learns a meaningful iterative computation, then depth becomes a resource you can adjust at inference time. And it can do that computation in its hidden state, without needing to turn every intermediate step into a token.

r001.rationale: It describes repeatedly applying the same block to a hidden state, capturing recurrent depth with shared layers.

r002.rationale: It says computation can increase without growing the model and that intermediate steps need not become tokens, communicating extra hidden computation decoupled from output generation.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that recurrence separates the number of parameters from the amount of computation you do. In a standard transformer, if you want more depth, you generally add more layers, and each layer has its own parameters. With recurrence, you can apply the same block repeatedly, so you can do more computation without making the model larger.

That gives you a different way to think about depth: as iterations of an algorithm. The model has a hidden state, it updates that state, and then it gets another opportunity to refine it. The interesting question is whether it learns a computation that actually benefits from those extra iterations, rather than just learning to work at one fixed depth.

And then you can ask whether every input needs the same amount of computation. Maybe something simple needs only a few iterations, while something harder benefits from many more. So recurrence opens up this possibility of adapting the computation to the problem, while keeping the underlying model fixed.

r001.rationale: It says recurrence applies the same block repeatedly, using shared parameters across iterations.

r002.rationale: It describes extra iterations and computation while keeping the model fixed, but does not say this computation occurs before producing the next output or is decoupled from output generation.
